Description: A small black agate seal, about the size of a thumbnail and pierced like a bead so its owner could wear it and press it into wet clay as a signature, found in a tomb at Tell en-Nasbeh (identified as biblical Mizpah) during the Badè excavations of 1926–1935. In Hebrew letters of the 6th century BCE it reads 'Belonging to Jaazaniah, Officer of the King' (ebed ha-melekh, servant or officer of the king). The fighting cock on the lower part of the seal is one of the oldest representations of the rooster found in Israel/Palestine.
Interpretations: The seal itself is certain, but its owner is not: it is possible, not proven, that this seal belonged to the army captain Jaazaniah who came to Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BCE (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8), as the museum panel and Walter Kaiser suggest. The name Jaazaniah belonged to several biblical figures, including Jaazaniah son of Shaphan (Ezekiel 8:11), a different man, so the seal must not be assigned to a biblical figure without the 'possible' qualifier. Its value stands regardless: it shows a royally titled official named Jaazaniah operating at Mizpah in exactly the generation of Gedaliah's governorship.
AlternativeNames: Seal of Yaazanyahu, Servant of the King
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
BiblicalSignificance: It puts a named royal officer at Mizpah in the months after Jerusalem's fall, matching the world of Gedaliah's governorship in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 40.
CurrentLocation: Badè Museum of Biblical Archaeology, Berkeley, California (Tell en-Nasbeh collection)
